coauthors.name: Samuel D. Soskin
coauthors.bio: Rabbi Samuel D. Soskin (1905–1970) born in Cleveland, Ohio, was a civil rights activist and Reform movement rabbi in the United States. He attended Western Reserve University and the University of Cincinnati before graduating from Hebrew Union College in 1932. In 1936, he took the pulpit at Congregation Beth El (Fort Worth, Texas) where he also served on many local community and religious groups. Besides his congregational work, he served as director of the Fort Worth Opera Guild and a chaplain and counselor at the United States Public Health Service Hospital. Soskin warned the community about the menace abroad and likened the Nazis’ early restrictions against Jews to Jim Crow laws in the southern United States. He was also among the founders in 1943 of Fort Worth’s Planned Parenthood chapter. During World War Ⅱ he was a chaplain in the Navy and one of his tours of duty was at the Manhattan Beach Coast Guard Station. He was later assigned to the South Pacific. In 1949, to came to Temple Beth Emeth (Flatbush, Brooklyn, New York). He served as national chair of CCAR’s Commission of Justice and Peace in the 1960s and led a group of rabbis who joined the Freedom March in Birmingham, Alabama. He also was a member of the social justice committee of the Union of American Hebrew Congregations. He contributed to many religious publications and was the first editor of Social Action in Review, a publication of the Union of American Hebrew Congregations.

coauthors.bio: The Congressional Record is the official record of the proceedings and debates of the United States Congress, published by the United States Government Printing Office and issued when Congress is in session. Indexes are issued approximately every two weeks. At the end of a session of Congress, the daily editions are compiled in bound volumes constituting the permanent edition. Statutory authorization for the Congressional Record is found in Chapter 9 of Title 44 of the United States Code. (wikipedia)

content:
Guest Chaplain: Rabbi Samuel Soskin, Temple Beth Emeth, Brooklyn, N.Y.
Sponsor: n/a
Date of Prayer: 1 March 1951

Contribute a translation Source (English)
“Proclaim liberty throughout the land
unto all the inhabitants thereof.”[1] The English translation of a portion of Leviticus 25:10 as engraved on the Liberty Bell.  (Leviticus 25:10)
May these sacred words,
O Heavenly Father,
touch our souls
as we seek guidance
in a day of difficulty.[2] Reference uncertain. In the context of the Cold War, it may refer to the impending trial of Julius and Ethel Rosenberg on 6 March 1951 for espionage (arrested 17 July 1950). Following lines in this prayer, concerned with security, freedom, and their betrayal, seem to me to suggest this. –ANV 
From of old our country
builded by men and women
of invincible will
has served as eloquent symbol
of that liberty
so desperately sought by mankind.
Pioneers and workers
with spirits seared by tyranny
have come here for refuge and safety.
In gratitude for that refuge
they have cemented even more strongly
the free institutions of our beloved Nation.
Help us, O Lord,
to keep secure
those very institutions
they cherished.
May we never allow
the siren calls
of ambition
or of complacency
to drown out the voice of liberty
and thus cause betrayal
of a noble legacy.
Kindle in us the fire
which flames against
any and all oppression
and cuts through the chains
which enslave men.
Yea, may our very deeds and words
be so acceptable before Thee
that they will “proclaim liberty
throughout the land
unto all the inhabitants thereof.” (Leviticus 25:10)
Amen.

This prayer of the guest chaplain was offered in the third month of the first session of the 82nd US House of Representatives, and published in the Congressional Record, vol. 97 part 2 (1 March 1951), p. 1741.

Source(s)

Prayer of the Guest Chaplain – Samuel Soskin (House of Representatives, 1 March 1951), p. 1741
